title: Heat a thin layer of liquid from below and it tiles itself into cells

cover.alt: A layer of oil dusted with aluminium powder, its surface divided into a mesh of rounded polygonal cells.

body: Warm liquid is less dense than cool liquid, so a layer heated from below is top-heavy. At first the liquid's stickiness wins and heat simply seeps upwards. Past a threshold, though, the layer suddenly starts to churn, and the random motion organises itself into a regular pattern of rolling **Bénard cells**, often close to hexagons. For a layer between two plates, that threshold is a critical Rayleigh number of 1,708, a figure that weighs buoyancy against the liquid's resistance to flow.

slides.alt: Close-up of a layer of oil with aluminium powder in it. Smooth, swirling streaks slowly break up into a mesh of rounded polygonal cells that sharpen over time.
slides.caption: Aluminium powder in a layer of oil shows the flow: smooth swirls break up into a mesh of polygonal convection cells.

Warm, lighter liquid tends to rise

slides.question: Henri Bénard studied his cells in 1900. In what year did theory finally match his experiment?
slides.explanation: 1958. Lord Rayleigh's 1916 theory explained convection driven by temperature alone, but it didn't match what Bénard had seen until John Pearson brought in surface tension.

events.text: James Thomson sees cooling soapy water tiled
He shows the tiles are convection cells
Henri Bénard reaches it on his own
Lord Rayleigh works out the theory

slides.heading: The twist: surface tension
slides.text: Rayleigh's sums lost touch with Bénard's set-up, where the liquid had a free surface. Warmer liquid has weaker surface tension, so the surface is pulled towards cooler patches, and that helps drive the cells. That version is now called Bénard–Marangoni convection.
